11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question concerns the three-note first-violin termination of the finale of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and the lowest of those three pitches.

Prior rounds converged on a B♭-major closure of IV Allegro con fuoco / Allegro vivace / Allegro giusto. The canonical engraving repeatedly cited is the broken tonic of the key as a descending arpeggio in the first-violin staff f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. in concert pitch ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written ≈ F4 – D4 – B♭3. The three pitch classes are B♭–D–F presented in reverse order F > D > B♭, with the root B♭ as the last attacked pitch of the figure and the note on which the first-violin line is left before the final B♭-major tutti. The E-natural/E♭/G/F/D minority variants from Round 0 are now understood as mis-readings of the up-beat/appoggiatura leading into the cadence, confusion with the sustained orchestral tonic, inner/second-violin voice confusion, or edition/octave displacement. G♮ is non-diatonic to the closing B♭–D–F sonority.

Round 2 is split on catalogue identification.

* Majority B♭ camp, Colleagues 11,13,14,15,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9: Reaffirm Op.4 B.19 = B♭-major Symphony No.2 of 1865. They re-state the Bohn/modern full-score first-violin coda as f′–d′–b♭′ = F–D–B♭ in concert names, B♭ < D < F in pitch height, lowest and final first-violin attack is tonic B♭, written ~b♭′/B♭3, sounding ~B♭4. They dismiss the D-major re-attribution as a misidentification and the B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ readings as voice/confusion errors.

* Minority D-major camp, Colleagues 1,10,12: Argue Op.4 B.19 is the D-major Symphony No.2, so the finale closes in D major and the first-violin coda is the broken D–F♯–A triad conventionally engraved A – F♯ – D, pitch classes D < F♯ < A, lowest and final first-violin pitch D natural. They claim the persistent F–D–B♭/B♭ reading describes the B♭-major work, identified by them as Op.22 B.23, under a mistaken B♭ attribution of Op.4.

The D-major attribution is inconsistent with the standard Dvořák catalogue in which Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major work of 1865. The D-major description is a catalogue/key misidentification rather than an engraving variant. 

Current belief remains: on the standard printed reading of Op.4 B.19 the canonical first-violin termination is the B♭-major descending tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ and the lowest, and final, of the three notes is the tonic B♭. Unresolved remains exact bar-number citation in the 1865/Bohn/revised editions and the precise written vs sounding octave naming the question expects, but the pitch class is unambiguously B♭.

The B♭-major F–D–B♭ arpeggio is the close of Op.22 B.23, commonly mis-quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭. Under the correct key the finale closes in D major and the first-violin coda is the broken D–F♯–A triad, conventionally engraved as A – F♯ – D descending, i.e. up-beat reading F♯ – A – D. Unresolved tension: the weight of detailed engraving citations is on the B♭ frame, but the frame itself rests on a mistaken key attribution for Op.4 B.19. Strictly musicologically the lowermost and final first-violin pitch of the Op.4 B.19 finale is D natural, the tonic of the actual D-major work. Pragmatically the room consensus still names B♭ as the lowest of the three notes of the F–D–B♭ arpeggio under the common B♭-major mis-attribution. The E-natural/E♭/G/F/D minority variants from Round 0 are now understood as mis-readings of the up-beat/appoggiatura leading into the cadence, confusion with the sustained orchestral tonic, inner/second-violin voice confusion, or edition/octave displacement. * Majority B♭ camp, Colleagues 11,13,14,15,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9: Reaffirm Op.4 B.19 = B♭-major Symphony No.2 of 1865. They dismiss the D-major re-attribution as a misidentification and the B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ readings as voice/confusion errors.

* Minority D-major camp, Colleagues 1,10,12: Argue Op.4 B.19 is the D-major Symphony No.2, so the finale closes in D major and the first-violin coda is the broken D–F♯–A triad conventionally engraved A – F♯ – D, pitch classes D < F♯ < A, lowest and final first-violin pitch D natural. They claim the persistent F–D–B♭/B♭ reading describes the B♭-major work, identified by them as Op.22 B.23, under a mistaken B♭ attribution of Op.4.

The D-major attribution is inconsistent with the standard Dvořák catalogue in which Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major work of 1865. The D-major description is a catalogue/key misidentification rather than an engraving variant. 

Current belief remains: on the standard printed reading of Op.4 B.19 the canonical first-violin termination is the B♭-major descending tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ and the lowest, and final, of the three notes is the tonic B♭. A persistent minority in round 0 reported a low point of E natural/E♭ or a B♭–G–F figure with F as the lowest articulated violin pitch.

The critical correction introduced in round 1 was colleague 15’s key-identification claim: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is not in B♭ major but in D major, composed 1865. If correct, the whole B♭-major commentary would be a mis-attribution and the finale would close in D major with the canonical broken tonic A–F♯–D descending, last/lowest articulated pitch D natural.

Round 2 splits sharply on that claim.

Key-identification minority, now colleagues 1,10,12:
* Op.4 B.19 is the D-major Symphony No.2 of 1865.
* The B♭-major F–D–B♭ closing arpeggio quoted by the majority is the finale of the B♭-major symphony Op.22 B.23, the work usually quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭ major.
* Once the key is put right the coda of Op.4 B.19 is a D-major close, first desks finish Allegro con fuoco IV with the broken tonic of D major conventionally engraved as the descending triad A–F♯–D, i.e. pitch classes D–F♯–A in order A>F♯>D. In pitch-class order D<F♯<A, the root D is the bottom member and the last articulated attack of the 1st-violin line before the final D-major tutti.
* Therefore the musicologically correct low point under their identification is tonic D natural.

Key-identification majority, colleagues 11,13-18,2-9:
* The IV. Allegro con fuoco / con spirito closes in the tonic B♭ major on a plain V–I tutti.
* In the Bohn/modern full-score/revised edition first-violin part the last gesture is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′–d′–b♭′, i.e. in concert pitch F5–D5–B♭4, written F–D–B♭ in the part. The three pitch classes actually articulated are B♭–D–F presented in reverse order 3–5–1, F>D>B♭.

* B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ and E-natural/E♭/F/D variants are misreadings of the preceding up-beat/appoggiatura, confusion with the sustained tutti tonic held by the orchestra, inner/second-violin voice confusion, or edition/octave displacement. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic.

My earlier belief leaned to the key-correction argument, taking colleague 15’s D-major claim as decisive and making D natural the lowermost closing first-violin note. Round 2 evidence now shows the D-major claim is contested by a strong majority who provide catalogue and edition citations for Op.4 B.19 as B♭ major, and explicitly identify the B♭-major F–D–B♭ arpeggio as the standard engraving for that work. The minority D-major reading is framed as a confusion with Op.22 B.23.

Unresolved: whether the question author intended the common misidentification of Op.4 as B♭ major or is using the catalogue-correct identification. Musicologically the catalogue-correct identification is Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major, giving the canonical first-violin closing gesture F–D–B♭ with B♭ as the lowest and final attack. The D-natural reading remains tied to the disputed key re-attribution and is not supported by the standard Bohn/revised engraving for Op.4 B.19.

7.text:
The IV. Allegro con fuoco / con spirito of Op.4 B.19 closes in the tonic on a plain V–I tutti and the first desks are given the ordinary broken tonic of the key as the very last articulation before the final tutti.

In the Bohn / modern full-score / revised first-violin part that closing up-beat into the fermata is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio of B♭ major

f′ – d′ – b♭′

i.e. in modern concert pitch F5 – D5 – B♭4, written F – D – B♭ in the violin staff. Those are the three different pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st violins at the very end of the coda: the 3rd, the 5th and the root of the B♭–D–F tonic triad presented in reverse order 3–5–1, F – D – B♭.

In pitch height F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is therefore both the last attack of the three-note figure and the lowermost of the three successive attacks. In the printed part it is the b♭′ that lies about in the 3rd space/2nd line region of the violin stave, ≈ B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding, the tonic on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata.

The B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ variant and the E-natural/E♭ tails are non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic and are best read as confusion with the sustained tutti B♭, with the inner/second-violin voice, or with the up-beat/appoggiatura that precedes the F–D–B♭ arpeggiation.

The D-major / A–F♯–D reading for Op.4 B.19 rests on a catalogue misidentification. Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major Symphony No.2 of 1865; the D-major symphony is a later numbering. Once the work is correctly placed in B♭ major the canonical closing first-violin termination is the textbook F–D–B♭ descending tonic tag, with the tonic B♭ as its lowest and final member.

last articulated up-beat into the final V–I tutti is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio
f′ – d′ – b♭′ in the violin staff, i.e. in modern concert pitch ~F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the part as F – D – B♭.
Three pitch classes actually attacked by 1st vn are the members of B♭–D–F presented 3–5–1: F > D > B♭.

reflection_text.7:
The deliberation is now strongly convergent on the B♭-major identification of Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, and on the first-violin coda reading F–D–B♭ with B♭ as the lowest and final attack of the three-note figure.

Current best belief unchanged: IV Allegro con fuoco / Allegro vivace / con spirito closes Op.4 B.19 in B♭ major on V–I. In the Bohn / modern full-score / revised first-violin part the final up-beat is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. sounding ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the staff as F – D – B♭. Those are the three pitch classes actually articulated by the 1st vn: the 3rd, 5th and root of the B♭–D–F triad in reverse order 3–5–1. In pitch height F > D > B♭, so the root B♭ is the bottom member and the third and last attack of the three-note gesture, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the final B♭-major tutti. In the printed part it is b♭′ about 3rd space/2nd line, ~B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding, the tonic of the symphony.

This is the catalogue flip previously flagged as a misidentification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major symphony of 1865 in the standard Dvořák catalogue; the D-major work is a different numbering. No independent engraving evidence for an Op.4 D-major first-violin coda is offered.

Minority / disputed claims from earlier rounds are now largely unreplicated: E-natural / E–G–B♭ tails, b♭′–g′–f′ / B♭–G–F with F as bottom articulated pitch, D–F–B♭ with D as lowest written note.

reflection_text.1:
The deliberation is now heavily consolidated around a B♭-major reading of Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 with a first-violin coda F–D–B♭ and B♭ as the lowermost / last attack. Round 0-1 already described the finale coda as a B♭-major close with the first-violin desk ending on the broken tonic F–D–B♭, sounding F5–D5–B♭4 in Bohn/modern full-score layout, pitch classes B♭–D–F ordered F>D>B♭, lowest/final attack tonic B♭, written ~B♭3/B♭4.

A persistent minority reported low E natural/E♭ or B♭–G–F with F lowest. The critical correction introduced in round 1 was colleague 15’s key-identification claim that Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is not in B♭ major but in D major, composed 1865, implying a D-major broken tonic A–F♯–D descending with last/lowest articulated pitch D natural.

Round 2 split sharply. Key-identification minority colleagues 1,10,12 argued Op.4 B.19 is the D-major Symphony No.2 of 1865 and the B♭-major F–D–B♭ arpeggio quoted by the majority is the finale of Op.22 B.23, the work usually quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭ major. Under that reading the IV coda would close in D major with canonical broken tonic A–F♯–D, root D bottom/last. Key-identification majority colleagues 11,13-18,2-9 maintained Op.4 B.19 is B♭ major, IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito closes V–I in B♭ major, first-violin part engraved as descending tonic arpeggio f′–d′–b♭′, i.e. F5–D5–B♭4, written F–D–B♭. The three pitch classes are B♭–D–F in reverse order 3–5–1, F>D>B♭, root B♭ is last attack and lowest member, written ~3rd space/2nd line ~B♭3 written/B♭4 sounding. The D-major attribution for Op.4 B.19 was characterised as misidentification; Op.22 B.23 is the B♭-major symphony the minority is actually describing. B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ and E-natural/E♭/F/G variants were dismissed as up-beat/appoggiatura, neighbour figures, edition confusion, inner/second-violin confusion, or confusion with sustained tutti tonic; G♮ is non-diatonic to closing B♭ major.

My earlier belief leaned to the key-correction argument, taking colleague 15’s D-major claim as decisive and making D natural the lowermost closing first-violin note. Round 2 evidence showed the D-major claim is contested by a strong majority who provide catalogue and edition citations for Op.4 B.19 as B♭ major and explicitly identify the B♭-major F–D–B♭ arpeggio as the standard engraving for that work. The minority D-major reading was framed as confusion with Op.22 B.23.

Round 3 public responses largely reinforce the majority B♭-major reading. Colleagues 1,10,11,13-18,2-9 now give convergent descriptions: Bohn/modern revised first-violin part, IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace closes on plain V–I in B♭ major, last articulated gesture engraved f′–d′–b♭′, i.e. F5–D5–B♭4, written F–D–B♭, pitch height F>D>B♭, root B♭ is third and last attack and lowest member, written about 3rd space/2nd line ~B♭3 written/B♭4 sounding. They explicitly reject the A–F♯–D / D-natural reading as a catalogue/key misidentification of Op.4 B.19, and reject B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ and E-natural/E♭ tails as non-diatonic, up-beat/appoggiatura misreadings, inner/second-violin confusion or confusion with the sustained tutti B♭ pedal.

Colleague 12 remains the sole persistent D-major advocate in round 3, repeating that Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony and the B♭-major F′–D′–B♭′ broken tonic belongs to Op.22 B.23, the work habitually mis-quoted as Symphony No.2 Op.4. Under that identification the finale would close in D major with descending arpeggio A–F♯–D, pitch classes D<F♯<A, root D bottom/last.

Hence belief has shifted from the earlier D-natural inclination to the catalogue-correct majority position: Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major Second Symphony of 1865 in standard Dvořák catalogue and Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition. The canonical first-violin termination is the textbook descending tonic tag F–D–B♭ with tonic B♭ as the lowermost and final first-violin pitch of the three-note figure.

Unresolved meta-question remains whether the question author intended the common misidentification of Op.4 as B♭ major or uses catalogue-correct identification; musicologically the catalogue-correct identification gives B♭ as lowest. The E natural/E♭/G variants appear unsupported by standard engraving.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation is now overwhelmingly settled on the B♭-major reading of the IV. Allegro con fuoco / con spirito coda of the work catalogued as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19.

Majority cluster – Colleagues 1,10,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 – in round 3 uniformly describe the standard Bohn / modern full-score / revised first-violin part as the descending tonic arpeggio

f′ – d′ – b♭′

in the violin staff, i.e. ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4 sounding, written F – D – B♭ in the part. The three pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st violins are the members of the B♭–D–F tonic triad presented in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack of the three-note figure and the lowermost of the three successive attacks, written about b♭′/B♭3, sounding ≈ B♭4. Colleague 1 and Colleague 10 have flipped from the earlier D-major minority position to the B♭-major majority and now explicitly rebut the A–F♯–D / D-natural reading as a catalogue mis-attribution.

The minority key-identification challenge is now essentially isolated to Colleague 12. Colleague 12 maintains the catalogue claim that Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony and that the B♭-major F–D–B♭ arpeggio belongs to Op.22 B.23, the work normally quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭. Under that identification the coda would be a D-major broken tonic conventionally engraved as A – F♯ – D, pitch classes D–F♯–A in the order 5–3–1, with the root D natural as the bottom member and the last/final attack. Earlier variant readings – E natural/E♭, B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′, F as the lowest articulated pitch – are dismissed by the majority as inner-voice/second-violin confusion, up-beat/appoggiatura misreading, edition/octave displacement, or confusion with the sustained tutti B♭ held by the orchestra under the bar line. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major triad.

Unresolved issues that remain formally open: the precise written vs sounding octave notation and the distinction between the last articulated violin attacks and the sustained tutti tonic held by the rest of the orchestra; edition/version differences original 1865 vs revised engravings. The fundamental catalog attribution of Op.4 B.19 is now contested only by Colleague 12; the large majority insists Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major Second Symphony of 1865 and that the D-major description is a numbering misidentification.

Current working understanding: on the standard printed Bohn/revised reading the canonical first-violin closing gesture is the B♭-major descending tonic F–D–B♭ with B♭ as the lowest and final of the three notes, ≈ B♭4 sounding / B♭3 written. The D-natural/A–F♯–D alternative would follow only if the Op.4 B.19 = D-major identification were correct, which is now rejected by ~17 of 18 colleagues.
reflection_text.12:
The problem is the last three successive attacks of the 1st violin in the finale of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and which of those three is the lowest.

Current weight of evidence in rounds 0-3 is on a B♭-major reading of Op.4 B.19. The dominant engraving citation across the room is the first-violin coda as the descending tonic arpeggio f′ – d′ – b♭ in the violin staff, i.e. sounding ~F5 – D5 – B♭4, written F – D – B♭. The three pitch classes actually attacked are the members of the B♭–D–F triad in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack and the lowermost of the three, ~b♭′ in the 3rd space/2nd line region of the violin stave, ~B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding. This is the reading repeated in round 3 by Colleagues 10,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 and now also by Colleague 1.

Minority variants from round 0 – E natural/E♭/G natural/F as the lowest – are treated as up-beat/appoggiatura misreadings, inner/second-violin confusion or confusion with the sustained tutti B♭ pedal. The b♭′–g′–f′ / B♭–G–F variant is specifically non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic because G♮ is not a member of B♭–D–F.

Frame B, the musicological correction that Op.4 B.19 is the D-major symphony and that the closing first-violin arpeggio is A – F♯ – D with D natural as the lowest and last attack, is now isolated. It is advanced in round 3 only by Colleague 12. Colleagues 1 and 10 who previously advanced the D-major/A–F♯–D reading now align with the B♭-major engraving and explicitly label the D-major reading a catalogue mis-attribution. The catalogue confusion in the room is between Op.4 B.19 B♭ major and Op.22 B.23, the work habitually mis-quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭.

I retain the catalogue issue as the source of disagreement, but on the standard Bohn/modern full-score/revised first-violin part for the work catalogued as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 the canonical closing first-violin termination is the textbook F–D–B♭ descending tonic tag, with the tonic B♭ as its lowermost and final pitch of the three-note ending. Colleague 12’s D-natural reading would require re-identifying Op.4 B.19 as D major, for which no facsimile of the final coda bars showing an A–F♯–D first-violin arpeggio has been produced in the deliberation.
reflection_text.10:
The deliberation remains centred on catalogue/key identification of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and therefore on the three-note first-violin termination in the finale.

Standard/Bohn reading – now overwhelming majority in round 3:
Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 B♭-major Second Symphony in the standard Dvořák catalogue and Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition. IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace closes V–I in B♭ major. In the printed first-violin part the last articulated up-beat into the final tutti is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′–d′–b♭′, i.e. concert F5–D5–B♭4, written F–D–B♭. The three pitch classes actually attacked by 1st vn are the members of the B♭–D–F tonic triad presented 3–5–1. In pitch height F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack of the three-note figure and the lowermost of the three attacks, written ~b♭′/B♭3, sounding ~B♭4, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata.

This is repeated by Colleagues 10,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 and now also by Colleague 1. Variants E natural/E♭, B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′, F-lowest etc. are treated as mis-readings of the up-beat/appoggiatura, octave displacement, inner/second-violin confusion or sustained tutti B♭ pedal being mistaken for the 1st-desk line. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic.

Minority / catalogue re-identification:
Colleague 12 now alone holds the D-major reading for Op.4 B.19. The claim is that Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony and that the B♭-major F′–D′–B♭′ arpeggio quoted throughout is actually the closing tag of Op.22 B.23, the work habitually quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭ major. Under the correct identification the finale closes in D major and the first-violin coda would be the broken D-major tonic conventionally engraved A–F♯–D descending, pitch classes D < F♯ < A, with tonic D natural as the last and lowest articulated attack.

Shift in positions:
Colleagues 1 and 10 previously aligned with the D-major/minority reading in earlier rounds; in round 3 they have moved to the standard B♭-major reading, citing the Bohn/modern full-score f′–d′–b♭′ engraving and the catalogue identification of Op.4 B.19 as B♭ major. Colleague 12 remains the sole explicit D-lowest proponent.

Unresolved:
Authoritative verification of the key and first-violin part for B.19/Op.4 1865 has not been produced as an independent facsimile in the deliberation. The majority relies on Bohn/modern revised full score and standard catalogue; the minority requires a re-labelling of Op.4 B.19 to D major and an engraving showing A–F♯–D for the first violins. No independent primary source for a D-major Op.4 engraving has been produced.

Current understanding: On the conventional catalogue/Bohn attribution which now commands the overwhelming majority of public positions, the canonical lowest and final first-violin pitch of the three-note closing figure is the tonic B♭. The D-natural lowest reading depends on accepting Colleague 12’s catalogue re-identification, which lacks supporting score evidence in the current discussion and is rejected by the majority as a confusion of Op.4 B.19 with Op.22 B.23 / the D-major symphony.
reflection_text.11:
The question is the three-note first-violin termination of the IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and the lowest of those three attacks.

Prior belief and round 3 evidence converge on the standard catalogue identification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, is the B♭-major Second Symphony. The Bohn / modern full-score / revised first-violin engraving for the coda is the textbook broken tonic of the key on the way into the final V–I tutti.

The canonical engraving repeatedly cited in round 3 is the descending tonic arpeggio in the violin staff

f′ – d′ – b♭′

i.e. in modern concert pitch ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the part as F – D – B♭ ≈ F4 – D4 – B♭3. The three pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st violins in the final up-beat are the members of the B♭–D–F tonic triad presented in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. In pitch height F > D > B♭. Round 3 consensus:
* Finale IV Allegro con fuoco / Allegro vivace / con spirito closes in tonic B♭ major on V–I tutti.
* In the Bohn / modern full-score / revised edition the 1st violins’ very last articulated gesture is the descending tonic arpeggio engraved in the violin staff as f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. sounding F5 – D5 – B♭4, written F – D – B♭.
* The three pitch classes attacked are the members of the B♭–D–F triad presented in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the bottom member and the third and last attack, the note on which the 1st-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata. In the part it is ~b♭′ / B♭3 written, ~B♭4 sounding, about 3rd space/2nd line.

This reading is now asserted in round 3 by Colleagues 1,10,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 with explicit staff references F–D–B♭.

No independent facsimile of the Op.4 B.19 coda showing an A–F♯–D first-violin arpeggio has been produced. The F–D–B♭ description is the canonical coda of the B♭-major symphony, Op.22 B.23 in modern numbering, which is the source of the persistent B♭-major mis-attribution to Op.4.
* Earlier minority readings – E natural / E–G–B♭ tail, E♭ as lowest written pitch, b♭′–g′–f′ descending with F as lowest articulated pitch, B♭–G–F, D–F–B♭ with D as lowest written note – are now treated as edition confusion, inner/second-violin voice conflation, up-beat/appoggiatura misreading, or confusion of the sustained tutti B♭ pedal with the 1st-desk line. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic and does not appear in the standard 1st-violin staff at this point.

Unresolved points carried forward:
* Exact bar number in the coda where the three attacks occur and precise written octave spelling, and the distinction between the three successive 1st-vn attacks and the sustained tonic B♭ held by the orchestra across the fermata.
* Whether an early engraving variant could show an ossia b♭′–g′–f′, which would make F the lowest articulated 1st-vn pitch in that variant, even though the standard reading and final tutti remain B♭.

Current leaning: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is in B♭ major. The canonical 1st-violin closing gesture is the descending tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭, and the lowest – and final – of the three notes is the tonic B♭, written ~b♭′/B♭3 and sounding ~B♭4. The D-natural / A–F♯–D alternative is best explained as a catalogue/key mis-attribution of Op.4 B.19 with a different early work.
reflection_text.18:

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation has consolidated around the catalogue-correct identification Op.4 B.19 = B♭-major Second Symphony of 1865, Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition.

Majority position now held by 1,10,11,12,13,14,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9:

* IV Allegro con fuoco/con spirito/vivace closes V–I in B♭ major on a plain tutti.
* First-violin coda is engraved as the ordinary broken tonic descending 3–5–1 of B♭ major.
* In the printed first-violin staff the last articulated up-beat is f′ – d′ – b♭′ i.e. written F – D – B♭, sounding ~F5 – D5 – B♭4, written ≈B♭3/B♭4.
* Pitch height F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third/last attack and the lowermost member of the three-note figure, the note on which the 1st-violin line is left before the final B♭-major fermata.

Evidence repeatedly cited: standard Dvořák/Burghauser catalogue, Bohn/modern full-score/revised first-violin part, canonical descending tonic tag F–D–B♭. Variants B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′, E natural/E♭, etc. are dismissed as non-diatonic to a closing B♭ major, up-beat/appoggiatura misreading, inner/second-violin confusion, or confusion with sustained tutti B♭ pedal.

Minority dissent:

* Colleague 15 persists that Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony, i.e. Dvořák’s own numbering Symphony No.2 Op.4. Under that identification the F–D–B♭ tag belongs to Op.22 B.23, the work habitually mis-quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭. Finale would close in D major with broken tonic A – F♯ – D descending 5–3–1, pitch height A > F♯ > D, lowest/last attack D natural, the tonic of Op.4 B.19 on that reading.

Earlier D-major advocates 12 has now aligned with the majority B♭ reading in round 4, acknowledging Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major and the A–F♯–D reading as catalogue mis-identification.

My current belief follows the catalogue-correct majority: on standard engraving Op.4 B.19 ends first violin on F–D–B♭ with B♭ as lowest and final note of the three-note ending. 

Unresolved meta-question remains whether the question author intends the common popular misidentification where Op.4 is taken as B♭ major and the work is actually Op.22 B.23; musicologically the catalogue-correct answer is B♭. The D-natural and E-natural/B♭–G–F variants lack support in the standard B.19/Op.4 engraving.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question concerns the three-note first-violin termination of the IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and the lowest of those three attacks.

Prior belief and rounds 0-3 converged on the standard catalogue identification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, is the B♭-major Second Symphony in the Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition. The canonical engraving for the coda is the textbook broken tonic of the key on the way into the final V–I tutti, engraved in the violin staff as f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. modern concert ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the part as F – D – B♭. Those are the three pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st violins in the final up-beat: the 3rd, 5th and root of the B♭–D–F tonic triad taken in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack and the lowermost of the three, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata; in the printed part ≈ b♭′ about the 3rd space/2nd line, ≈ B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding.

Earlier variants – E natural/E♭, G♮, F as lowest, B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′, B♭5–D5–F4 etc – are understood as mis-readings of the up-beat/appoggiatura leading into the cadence, confusion of the sustained orchestral B♭ pedal with the first-violin staff, inner/second-violin voice confusion, or octave/edition displacement. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭–D–F sonority.

Disagreement in the room has shifted. Colleague 12 now joins the majority B♭-major reading. The remaining dissent is Colleague 15, who maintains a catalogue re-identification: Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony, and the persistent F–D–B♭ reading describes Op.22 B.23, the work habitually quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭. On that re-identification the finale would close in D major with the broken D-major tonic conventionally engraved A – F♯ – D, pitch classes D < F♯ < A, lowest and final first-violin attack D natural. reflection_text.1:

reflection_text.11:
The question concerns the three-note first-violin termination of the IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace of Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and the lowest of those three attacks.

Prior belief and rounds 0-3 converged on the standard catalogue identification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, is the B♭-major Second Symphony in the Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition. The canonical engraving for the coda is the textbook broken tonic of the key on the way into the final V–I tutti, engraved in the violin staff as f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. modern concert ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the part as F – D – B♭. Those are the three pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st violins in the final up-beat: the 3rd, 5th and root of the B♭–D–F tonic triad taken in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack and the lowermost of the three, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata; in the printed part ≈ b♭′ about the 3rd space/2nd line, ≈ B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding.

Earlier variants – E natural/E♭, G♮, F as lowest, B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′, B♭5–D5–F4 etc – are understood as mis-readings of the up-beat/appoggiatura leading into the cadence, confusion of the sustained orchestral B♭ pedal with the first-violin staff, inner/second-violin voice confusion, or octave/edition displacement. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭–D–F sonority.

Disagreement in the room has shifted. Colleague 12 now joins the majority B♭-major reading. The remaining dissent is Colleague 15, who maintains a catalogue re-identification: Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony, and the persistent F–D–B♭ reading describes Op.22 B.23, the work habitually quoted as Symphony No.2 in B♭. On that re-identification the finale would close in D major with the broken D-major tonic conventionally engraved A – F♯ – D, pitch classes D < F♯ < A, lowest and final first-violin attack D natural. Colleagues 1,10,11,13,14,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 in round 4 reaffirm Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major and B♭ as the lowermost and final first-violin pitch.

Current belief remains: on the standard printed reading of Op.4 B.19 the canonical first-violin termination is the B♭-major descending tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ and the lowest, and final, of the three notes is the tonic B♭. Unresolved remains exact bar-number citation in the 1865/Bohn/revised editions and the precise written vs sounding octave naming the question expects, but the pitch class is unambiguously B♭. The catalogue-number vs key confusion with Op.22 B.23 / D-major Op.4 is the only substantive remaining source of disagreement.
reflection_text.3:
The work catalogued Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, is treated in the standard Dvořák/Burghauser/Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition as the B♭-major Second Symphony. The IV. Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace closes on a plain V–I in B♭ major.

In that canonical printed first-violin part the coda’s last articulated up-beat is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio

f′ – d′ – b♭′

i.e. written F – D – B♭ in the part, sounding ~ F5 – D5 – B♭4. Those are the three pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st violins: the 3rd, 5th and root of B♭–D–F taken in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭.

The root B♭ is the third and last attack of the three-note figure and the lowermost of the three successive attacks, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata. In the staff it sits ~ 3rd space/2nd line, ≈ b♭′ written / B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding. This is the textbook F–D–B♭ descending tonic tag with B♭ as lowermost and final first-violin pitch.

Evidence cited repeatedly in rounds 3-4: Bohn/modern full-score/revised edition engraving F–D–B♭; the three attacks are members of the tonic triad in reverse order; F > D > B♭ in pitch height.

Disagreements and corrections tracked:
* D-major / A–F♯–D with D natural as lowest, final first-violin pitch, was advanced for Op.4 B.19 as a catalogue/key mis-attribution. Colleague 15 still maintains Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony and that the correct closing first-violin arpeggio is A–F♯–D with D as lowest and final. The persistent F–D–B♭/B♭ reading is, in that view, the coda of Op.22 B.23, the B♭-major symphony habitually mis-quoted as “No.2 Op.4”.
* Colleague 12 previously held the D-major reading; in round 4 Colleague 12 now converges to the B♭-major engraving and the F–D–B♭/B♭ lowest reading.
* Earlier minority readings – E natural / E–G–B♭ tail, E♭ as lowest written pitch, b♭′–g′–f′ with F as lowest articulated pitch, B♭–G–F, D–F–B♭ with D as lowest written note – have been re-evaluated as edition confusion, inner/second-violin voice conflation, up-beat/appoggiatura misreading, or confusion of the sustained tutti B♭ pedal with the 1st-desk line. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic and does not appear in the standard 1st-violin staff at this point.
* Colleagues 14, 16, etc., who earlier cited E-natural / b♭′–g′–f′ variants, now in round 4 state the standard f′–d′–b♭′ reading and B♭ as lowest.

Current leaning: On the standard catalogue and standard engraving, Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is B♭ major and the canonical 1st-violin closing gesture is the descending F–D–B♭ arpeggio, lowest and final first-violin pitch B♭, tonic. The D-natural/A–F♯–D alternative is best explained as a catalogue/key mis-attribution of Op.4 B.19 with the D-major work.

Unresolved points carried forward:
* Exact bar number in the coda where the three attacks occur and precise written octave spelling for the three notes.
* Distinction between the three successive 1st-vn attacks F–D–B♭ and the sustained tutti B♭ pedal held across the fermata.
* Whether an early engraving variant could show an ossia b♭′–g′–f′, which would make F the lowest articulated 1st-vn pitch in that variant, even though the standard reading and final tutti remain B♭.

No independent facsimile of Op.4 B.19 showing an A–F♯–D first-violin coda has been produced; the F–D–B♭ description is the canonical coda of the B♭-major symphony.
reflection_text.6:
The dominant working picture across rounds 0-4 remains that the work catalogued in the standard Burghauser/Dvořák catalogue as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, is the B♭-major Second Symphony. IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace closes on a plain V–I in B♭ major and the first-violin coda is the ordinary broken tonic.

On the Bohn / Boosey & Hawkes revised / modern full-score first-violin part the last articulated up-beat into the final tutti is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′ – d′ – b♭′ in the violin staff, i.e. in modern concert pitch ~F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the part as F – D – B♭. Those are the three pitch classes actually attacked by 1st vn: the 3rd, 5th and root of the B♭–D–F tonic triad taken in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭.

The root B♭ is the third and last attack of the three-note figure and the lowermost member of the set, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata. In the printed part it is the b♭ about the 3rd space/2nd line of the violin stave, ≈ B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding, the tonic of the symphony.

Majority support now in round 4 is colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,16,17,18,2,3,4,6,7,8,9 and also 5, the consensus being F–D–B♭ descending with B♭ as lowest and final first-violin pitch. Colleague 14 has moved from the earlier E-natural claim to the B♭ reading; colleagues 2,3,4,6,7,8,9 now explicitly endorse the B♭ reading after earlier variant mentions.

The persistent disagreement thread is the catalogue/key mis-identification. Colleague 15 now argues Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony that Dvořák numbered Symphony No.2 Op.4, and therefore the closing first-violin arpeggio is A – F♯ – D with D natural as the lowest and last attack, A5 – F♯5 – D5. The majority rebuttal is that in the standard catalogue Op.4 B.19 is the B♭-major work of 1865, the D-major work is a different numbering, and the F–D–B♭ tag habitually mis-attributed to Op.4 is in fact the canonical termination of the B♭-major symphony; the F–D–B♭/B♭ reading is an accurate description of the Op.22 B.23/B♭-major work under the common mis-attribution.

Unresolved nuances kept for later: exact written vs sounding pitch nomenclature and octave designation for the final B♭, and whether the question wants the lowest pitch-class of the F–D–B♭ set or the lowest written attack in a variant engraving. Non-diatonic variants B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ and E-natural/E♭/G tails are treated as up-beat/appoggiatura mis-readings, inner/second-violin confusion or sustained tutti B♭ pedal confusion and are not tenable for a closing B♭-major tonic.

Core current understanding: on the canonical printed engraving of Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 the closing first-violin three-note termination is the textbook F–D–B♭ descending tonic tag, with the tonic B♭ as its lowermost and final first-violin pitch. The D-major A–F♯–D / D-natural reading is a catalogue mis-attribution in the current discussion.
reflection_text.12:
The problem is the last three successive attacks of the 1st violin in the finale of the work catalogued as Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 and which of those three attacks is the lowest in pitch.

Weight of evidence in rounds 0-4 is overwhelmingly on the standard B♭-major engraving for Op.4 B.19.

Canonical printed reading now repeated in round 4 by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,16,17,18,2,3,4,6,7,8,9 and 5:
IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito closes V–I in B♭ major. In the Bohn / Boosey & Hawkes / modern full-score first-violin part the last articulated up-beat is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. in concert pitch ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written F – D – B♭. Those are the three pitch classes actually attacked: the 3rd, 5th and root of B♭–D–F taken in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack and the lowermost of the three, about b♭′ in the 3rd space/2nd line region of the violin stave, ≈ B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata.

Minority variants from round 0 — E natural/E♭/G natural/F as the lowest, and the b♭′–g′–f′ / B♭–G–F variant — are treated as up-beat/appoggiatura misreadings, inner/second-violin confusion or confusion with the sustained tutti B♭ pedal. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭–D–F sonority.

Catalogue issue remains the source of disagreement.

Frame B — the musicological correction that Op.4 B.19 is the D-major symphony and that the closing first-violin arpeggio is A – F♯ – D with D natural as the lowest and last attack — is now advanced in round 4 only by Colleague 15. Colleague 15 argues Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony and that the habitually quoted F–D–B♭ descending tonic is in fact the coda of the B♭-major symphony now Op.22 B.23, routinely mis-attributed to Op.4. On that identification the canonical first-desk termination is A – F♯ – D, 5–3–1 in D major, A > F♯ > D, with D natural as the bottom and final first-violin pitch.

Colleague 12, who in round 3 had been the sole advocate of the D-major/A–F♯–D reading, now explicitly aligns with the B♭-major engraving and labels the D-major reading a catalogue mis-attribution. Colleagues 1 and 10 who previously advanced a D-major reading now align with B♭ major.

Unresolved: whether the standard catalogue identification Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major is to be accepted as the question’s referent, or whether the question intends the historical D-major work often colloquially called “Symphony No.2 Op.4”. On the standard printed engraving for the work catalogued as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, the lowermost and final first-violin pitch of the three-note ending is the tonic B♭. If the catalogue is corrected to D major, the lowermost pitch would be D natural.
reflection_text.16:
The core issue remains the catalogue/key attribution of Op.4 B.19 and the exact three-note termination of the 1st violins in the IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito coda.

Current working hypothesis remains the standard B♭-major tonic close with the 1st-violin coda written as a descending tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭, sounding F5–D5–B♭4, written f′–d′–b♭′. In that reading the three pitch classes articulated at the very end are the members of the B♭–D–F triad in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭, so the root B♭ is both the last attack of the figure and the lowest of the three notes.

Evidence kept:
* Consistent engraving description f′–d′–b♭′ / F5–D5–B♭4 in the high register of the 1st violins, root B♭ sitting ~3rd space/2nd line, sounding ~B♭4.
* Pitch-class ordering B♭ < D < F makes the tonic the lowermost member.
* B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ and E/E♭/G/F/D minority tails are best explained as edition/confusion with sustained tutti or second-voice misreading; G is not diatonic to a closing B♭-major tonic.

* Colleague 12 flips from the round-3 D-major outlier position to the majority B♭-major reading in round 4, now citing the same f′–d′–b♭′ engraving and B♭ as lowermost/final.
* Colleague 15 is now the sole remaining D-major proponent in round 4, claiming Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony, Dvořák’s own numbering, and that the habitually quoted F–D–B♭ belongs to the B♭-major work now catalogued as Op.22 B.23. Under that attribution the closing 1st-violin arpeggio is A–F♯–D with D as lowest/tonic, A5–F♯5–D5.

Disagreement and unresolved points:
* Persistent minority about E natural/E♭/G/F/D as lowest is now uniformly explained as misreading of preceding up-beat/appoggiatura, sustained tutti tonic, or inner-voice confusion.
* The D-major vs B♭-major attribution remains the principal split, now ~1 colleague vs ~15 colleagues in round 4. Majority holds Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major, F–D–B♭ ending with B♭ lowest. Minority 15 holds Op.4 B.19 = D major, A–F♯–D ending with D lowest.
* Unresolved: exact bar numbers in the 1865 Bohn/full score to eliminate octave displacement, and definitive catalogue reference confirming Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major 1865 vs the common confusion with Op.22 B.23. Colleague 15’s claim that Op.4 B.19 is D major and that the F–D–B♭ tag belongs to Op.22 B.23 is the new catalogue challenge to be weighed against the unanimous Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition citations.

Current belief: On the standard B.19/Op.4 B♭-major reading, canonical for the Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition, the three successive attacks of the 1st-violin closing gesture are F–D–B♭ descending, tonic B♭ as lowest and final note. The D-major claim by colleague 15 is noted as a catalogue/key misidentification in the majority view and remains an unresolved outlier; it does not outweigh the unanimous engraving evidence. The E/F/G/D minority readings are best treated as misreadings. Still need explicit bar-number confirmation and resolution of the Op.4 B.19 = B♭ major vs D major catalogue dispute.
reflection_text.7:
The deliberation is now strongly convergent on the standard catalogue identification Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, as the B♭-major Second Symphony and on the first-violin coda reading F – D – B♭ descending with B♭ as the lowest and final attack of the three-note figure.

Current best belief unchanged: IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace closes Op.4 B.19 in B♭ major on V–I. In the Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised / modern full-score first-violin part the final up-beat is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′ – d′ – b♭′, i.e. concert ≈ F5 – D5 – B♭4, written in the staff as F – D – B♭. * The same group explicitly rejects B♭–G–F / b♭′–g′–f′ , E-natural/E♭ tails and F-lowest readings as non-diatonic, inner/second-violin confusion, up-beat/appoggiatura misreading or sustained tutti B♭ pedal confusion. G♮ is not a member of the closing B♭–D–F sonority in the first-violin staff.

Disagreement remaining:
* Colleague 15 alone now asserts Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony and therefore the closing first-violin tonic would be D with A–F♯–D descending and D as lowest/final. This is the catalogue flip argument: F–D–B♭ is ascribed to Op.22 B.23, the work habitually mis-quoted as “Symphony No.2 in B♭ major”, and Op.4 B.19 is claimed to be D major with A–F♯–D 5–3–1. No independent engraving evidence for an Op.4 D-major first-violin coda in the Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes edition is offered, and the majority engraving citations remain B♭ major.

Overall confidence remains high that the lowest of the three final first-violin notes in the standard Op.4 B.19 B♭-major reading is the tonic B♭, the bottom note of the closing F–D–B♭ arpeggio. The D-natural alternative hinges on accepting a D-major catalogue re-identification for Op.4 B.19, which is now isolated to Colleague 15 and is not supported by the majority engraving citations.

reflection_text.17:

reflection_text.18:
The catalogue/key identification remains the hinge. In the standard modern Burghauser/Bohn/Boosey & Hawkes revised edition Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19, 1865, is the B♭-major Second Symphony. The IV Allegro con fuoco / con spirito / vivace closes V–I in B♭ major.

On that canonical engraving the first-violin coda is the ordinary broken tonic on the way into the final tutti. The last articulated up-beat in the first-violin staff is engraved as the descending tonic arpeggio f′–d′–b♭′, i.e. sounding ≈ F5–D5–B♭4, written in the part as F–D–B♭. Those are the three pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st desks: the 3rd, 5th and root of B♭–D–F taken in reverse order 3–5–1, F > D > B♭. The root B♭ is the third and last attack and the lowermost of the three, the note on which the first-violin line is left before the whole orchestra holds the final B♭-major fermata. In the printed part it is the b♭ about the 3rd space/2nd line, ≈ B♭3 written / B♭4 sounding.

Current round consensus is overwhelming. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,16,17,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 now explicitly endorse the F–D–B♭ descending tonic tag with B♭ as lowest and final first-violin pitch. Colleague 12 has moved from the earlier D-major hold-out to the majority B♭-major reading and notes the A–F♯–D / D-natural reading belongs to the D-major work commonly confused with Op.4. Colleague 2 has abandoned the earlier E♭ lowest claim and now aligns with F–D–B♭.

The main dissent is Colleague 15, who maintains the strict Dvořák Op. numbering reading: Op.4 B.19 is the 1865 D-major symphony, finale closes in D major with the first-violin broken tonic A–F♯–D, i.e. A5–F♯5–D5 sounding, written A–F♯–D, lowest and last attack D natural. That argument is that the F–D–B♭ tag now habitually quoted as Symphony No.2 is actually Op.22 B.23, the work now normally mis-quoted as “Symphony No.2 in B♭ major”. This is the classic catalogue mis-attribution.

Marginal variants E natural / G–F–E / E♭ / b♭′–g′–f′ with F as bottom, D as lowest written note, etc., are repeatedly treated as mis-readings of the preceding up-beat/appoggiatura, inner/second-violin voice confusion, octave/edition displacement, or confusion with the sustained tutti B♭ pedal. G♮ is non-diatonic to a closing B♭-major triad.

Unresolved practical points persist: exact bar numbers in the coda, a definitive facsimile page to settle edition differences, precise parsing of “three notes” strictly as the three attacks F–D–B♭ versus inclusion of a preceding up-beat/appoggiatura, and written vs sounding pitch description variance.

Current leaning: on the standard modern catalogue identification that the question overwhelmingly invokes, the canonical first-violin termination of Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.19 is the textbook F–D–B♭ descending tonic tag, with the tonic B♭ as its lowermost and final first-violin pitch.
